title: Header and MethodTable
sub: What sits before the fields and how much an object weighs
cards/0/title: A reference does not point at the start of the object
cards/0/body:
In the Deeper C# course you saw two bookkeeping words in front of an object's fields. Now more precisely, for x64:

  • −8: the object header — 8 bytes, of which 4 are used and the other 4 are padding;
  • 0: the MethodTable pointer — 8 bytes. This is where the reference points;
  • +8: the instance fields.

The reference targets the type pointer because it is needed most often: a virtual call, a cast, GetType — one read at the reference address. The header is rarely needed, and it is one step back, at −8.
cards/0/deep:
In the runtime sources this is ObjHeader (file src/coreclr/vm/syncblk.h): on a 64-bit platform it has a padding field m_alignpad and a 32-bit m_SyncBlockValue. On x86 the header and the type pointer are 4 bytes each, and the minimum object is 12 bytes.

The header formally belongs to the object but sits "before" it. That is why the allocator zeroes memory ahead: the header of the next object is already zero when it gets allocated.
cards/1/q: What does the reference Order o point at in a 64-bit process?
cards/1/options/0: The word holding the MethodTable pointer inside the object
cards/1/options/3: Directly at the MethodTable of Order
cards/1/explain: A reference is the address of the type-pointer word. The header is 8 bytes earlier, the fields 8 bytes later. The MethodTable itself is a separate structure, one per type.
cards/1/wrong/1: The header sits at a negative offset: ref − 8.
cards/1/wrong/3: There is one MethodTable per type, and it lives outside the object heap. The object holds only a pointer to it.
cards/2/title: 32 header bits: one of three things
cards/2/body:
The top bits of the header are flags, and the rest of the space holds one of three things:

  • a thin lock: the owning thread id (16 bits) and the recursion depth (6 bits). This is how lock works while there is no contention;
  • the default hash code — 26 bits, written by RuntimeHelpers.GetHashCode (and by a non-overridden GetHashCode);
  • a sync block index — the number of an entry in the sync block table, a separate structure in native memory.

If an object needs more than fits in 32 bits — say, both a hash and a lock — the CLR gives it a sync block: it moves the hash and the monitor state there and writes the index into the header.
cards/2/deep:
The constants are in syncblk.h: BIT_SBLK_IS_HASH_OR_SYNCBLKINDEX says the low 26 bits hold a hash or an index, BIT_SBLK_IS_HASHCODE tells them apart. The BIT_SBLK_FINALIZER_RUN flag is set by GC.SuppressFinalize, and the collector uses BIT_SBLK_GC_RESERVE while it works, with all threads stopped.

The monitor also needs a sync block in its "heavy" state: threads waiting for the lock, a call to Monitor.Wait. The System.Threading.Lock type from .NET 9 does not touch another object's header: lock on it calls methods of the Lock object itself.
cards/3/pairs/0/1: Nobody locked the object or took its hash
cards/3/pairs/1/1: Owning thread id and recursion depth
cards/3/pairs/3/1: An entry number in a separate table
cards/4/q: After which line will the object definitely have a sync block?
cards/4/explain: The first lock is a thin lock in the header, released on exit. GetHashCode writes the hash into the now free header. The second lock has no room left: the CLR moves the hash into a sync block and writes the index into the header.
cards/5/body:
There is one MethodTable per type: a million Order objects hold a million pointers to the same structure. It lives not in the GC heap but in loader memory (the loader heap). It contains:

  • BaseSize — the instance size in bytes, header included;
  • ComponentSize — the element size for arrays and strings;
  • flags: does it have a finalizer, does it contain references, is it an array;
  • the parent, the interface map, the virtual method slots.

The collector needs the MethodTable all the time. From it, it learns the object size to step to the next object, and where the references inside are that must be traced.
cards/5/deep: The description of references — the GCDesc — sits right before the MethodTable, at negative offsets: a list of "series", ranges of the object where references follow one another. Rarely needed type data (field descriptors, links to metadata) is moved out to a separate EEClass structure. You can look at all of this in a debugger with the SOS extension: !dumpobj, !dumpmt. Each closed generic has its own MethodTable: List<int> and List<string> are different types.
cards/6/q: The collector walks the heap object by object. How does it know where the current object ends?
cards/6/options/0: From the MethodTable: BaseSize, plus length × ComponentSize for arrays and strings
cards/6/options/1: The object size is stored in its header
cards/6/options/2: The GC keeps a separate table with the sizes of all objects
cards/6/options/3: Objects in the heap are separated by zero markers
cards/6/explain: The size is not stored in the object: it follows from the type. For a plain object it is BaseSize; for an array or a string it is BaseSize plus the length times the element size, rounded up to 8 bytes.
cards/6/wrong/1: The header has only 32 bits of flags, hash and lock — no size.
cards/7/title: What is not in the object
cards/7/body:
Each instance holds only the header, the type pointer and the instance fields. Everything shared by the type is stored once:

  • static fields — in separate per-type memory, not in every object;
  • method code — machine code from the JIT, one per type;
  • the virtual method table — in the MethodTable.

So methods and statics do not make objects heavier. A million instances of a class with a hundred methods weigh the same as a million instances of a class with one method and the same fields.
cards/7/deep: Exactly how the runtime lays out statics has changed from version to version. One detail will be useful later: CoreCLR keeps a static struct field in a separate box — one box per field for the whole lifetime, and writes change its contents. In .NET 8 such boxes for structs without references moved to the non-GC heap — more on it in lesson 4.
cards/8/q: What is stored in every instance of Order? Select all.
cards/8/options/4: The slot of the virtual method Total
cards/8/explain: Count is a static field, there is one per type. The Total slot is in the MethodTable, not in the object. The instance holds 8 bytes of header, 8 bytes of type pointer, an int and a reference — 32 bytes in total.
cards/9/title: How much an object weighs: the arithmetic
cards/9/body:
The formula for a plain object on x64: 16 bytes (header and type pointer) + fields with alignment, the total rounded up to 8 and no less than 24 bytes.

  • new object() — 24: no fields, but nothing goes below the minimum;
  • a class with one int — 24: 16 + 4, rounded to 24;
  • a boxed int or long — 24;
  • a class with three int fields — 32: 16 + 12 = 28, rounded to 32.

You can check it with the thread's allocation counter: it counts bytes exactly.
cards/9/deep:
The 24-byte minimum is defined in the runtime as MIN_OBJECT_SIZE = two pointers + the header. One reason: in place of dead objects the collector leaves a "free object" — a fake array with its own type pointer and length, and it must fit into any gap.

Do not confuse this with Unsafe.SizeOf<T>(): for a class it returns 8 — the size of a reference, not of the object. For a struct it returns the size of its fields without a header.
cards/10/q: How many bytes does an object of this class take on the x64 heap?
cards/10/explain: 16 bytes of bookkeeping plus 12 bytes of fields is 28. Objects are aligned to 8 bytes, so it is 32.
cards/10/wrong/1: That is before alignment. On x64 an object size is always a multiple of 8.
cards/11/q: Measure how many bytes new Order() allocates
cards/11/explain: The thread counter grows by exactly the allocated size. GetTotalMemory shows an approximate heap size and depends on collections. KeepAlive stops the JIT from treating the object as unused — in .NET 9–10 it can place objects that never leave the method on the stack, and then the counter would show zero.
